primitives.name: Hierarchical Bayesian Model
primitives.verbatim_quote: Using multilevel models to estimate team ability is becoming more common and the goal of this post is to show how you can build your own model of EPA that will return regularized, opponent-adjusted measures of offensive and defensive EPA/play for each team.
primitives.assumptions: Normality of EPA errors, hierarchical prior structure on team abilities, independence of plays conditional on team identity, and exchangeability across seasons.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Breakdown occurs when small sample sizes lead to unreliable posterior means; regularization prevents overfitting but may overshrink true effects if priors are misspecified.

layer2.mapping: Bayesian hierarchical models correspond to Gaussian process regression with specific covariance structures, enabling exact probabilistic predictions and uncertainty quantification.
layer2.telemetry: Effective sample size diagnostics, posterior predictive checks, and cross-validation metrics to assess model fit.

primitives.name: Shrinkage Estimation
primitives.verbatim_quote: We can think of \(alpha_{ij}\) as our estimate of team ability and to build the model we will put some hierarchical priors on this estimate.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'alpha_ij': 'Team ability parameter (dimensionless)', 'sigma_off': 'Standard deviation of team abilities (dimensionless)', 'alpha_off_raw': 'Standard normal latent variable (dimensionless)'}
primitives.assumptions: Hierarchical normal structure, exchangeability of teams, and independence of ability parameters conditional on hyperparameters.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Excessive shrinkage occurs when true effects are sparse or have heavy tails, leading to biased estimates; insufficient shrinkage happens with high signal-to-noise ratios.

layer2.mapping: James-Stein estimators provide a closed-form solution for shrinkage in normal means problems, extending to generalized linear mixed models.
layer2.telemetry: Empirical Bayes estimates of hyperparameters via marginal likelihood maximization, and posterior variance as uncertainty measure.

reasoning_traces.think:
The core issue is that raw EPA/Play exhibits high variance due to small sample sizes and noisy measurements. Multilevel models address this by borrowing strength across teams, shrinking individual estimates toward a common distribution. This reduces mean squared error compared to ordinary least squares, especially for teams with few observations. However, if the hierarchical structure is misspecified or the data-generating process changes over time, these models can produce misleading inferences. The key trade-off is between bias introduced by regularization and variance reduction; optimal shrinkage balances this compromise.
